newsitem.title: USA: Quasars live at heart of colliding galaxies.
newsitem.headline: Quasars live at heart of colliding galaxies.

text.p: Quasars, the most powerful objects in the universe, are created at the heart of cannibalistic, colliding galaxies, astronomers working with the Hubble Space Telescope reported on Tuesday.
"Hubble has finally unmasked quasars for what they really are," astrophysicist John Bahcall said at a briefing at NASA headquarters. "Quasars will eat almost anything."
In previous decades scientists theorised that quasars might have existed as free-floating "naked" objects in space; the new Hubble images lay that theory to rest.

Bahcall and others said new images from the orbiting Hubble telescope show that quasars live almost symbiotically at the centre of galaxies, feeding on the surrounding galactic material and emitting as much as 1,000 times the energy of an entire galaxy in the space of a solar system like our own.

They shine brilliantly but scientists are trying to determine whether their brilliance is a cosmic flash-in-the-pan -- possibly as brief as 10 million years, a mere blink relative to the 15 billion years since the universe was born -- or more long-lived.

Quasars appear to co-exist in these galaxies with black holes -- small, dark, invisible features that nevertheless have the power to inhale all material around them, ultimately including the galaxy itself.

Hubble scientists do not know whether these black holes were always at the heart of these galaxies and only become evident when a galactic collision "switches on" a glowing quasar, or whether quasars and black holes are created from the same smash-up.

The latest images beamed down from Hubble show the crash of galaxies as a violent dance that often ends with the larger of the two gobbling up the smaller. The energy expended sends debris flying and creates the energy needed for quasars, the scientists said.

Prime time for galaxies to collide was perhaps 10 billion years ago, according to astronomer Mike Disney, who also spoke at the briefing at the National Aeronautics and Space Administration headquarters.
Without the interference encountered by even the best ground-based telescopes, the Hubble pictures give a clear picture of quasars, whose very brightness has been a hindrance to astronomic study.

Earlier images of quasars, which were discovered in 1963, showed a central bright spot with a halo of fuzz, leading some scientists to theorise quasars were "naked" -- that is, existed apart from a large astronomic feature such as a galaxy.

The new Hubble images show quasars as within recognisable galaxies, Bahcall said, proving that while there may be some "lightly-clothed" quasars existing in smaller galaxies, there is little sign of quasars actually "naked". Of the 20 quasars Bahcall's team observed, all were surrounded by galaxies.
But of those 20, only three were classic collisions. The others managed to spawn quasars after relatively peaceful mergers, the scientists said.
Quasars themselves are quite rare: only one galaxy in a million has a quasar.
Future studies are expected to focus on what kinds of galaxies are most likely to have quasars at their hearts.
